newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian CPI dips but rate cut seen unlikely.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian CPI dips but rate cut seen unlikely.

text.p: Italian inflation dipped to 1.6 percent year-on-year in May, its lowest level since February 1969, national statistics office Istat said on Wednesday, though the figure was at the top end of market expectations.

Analysts said they did not expect this latest fall to trigger an immediate Bank of Italy rate cut, despite widespread calls for a reduction in the cost of money to boost the flagging economy and ease the state's huge debt servicing bill.
Preliminary data from 11 sample cities had pointed to the consumer price index rising 1.5 or 1.6 percent year-on-year for May against 1.7 percent in April and 4.3 percent in May 1996.
Month-on-month inflation rose 0.3 percent, with an increase in postal charges weighing heavily. Other key components in the inflation basket, such as food, remained little changed.
"If there was some remaining hope that the Bank of Italy could respond to the May inflation figure, that has now receded," said Riccardo Barbieri, senior economist at Morgan Stanley in London.
The Bank of Italy has dropped its official discount rate by 2.25 percentage points since last July, with the last cut coming in January. The discount rate stands at 6.75 percent.

Many analysts had expected a further reduction in recent weeks given the steady fall in inflation since the start of the year, but Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio dampened expectations in a keynote speech on Saturday.
The central bank chief warned that although Italian inflationary expectations had been beaten, "the flames of inflation have not been completely extinguished".
He added that he would not hesitate to tighten monetary policy at the first hint of a reawaking of inflation.

"The problem for Fazio is that the fall in inflation has been strongly tied to weakness in the economic cycle and he wants to see what will happen with the expected pick-up," said Riccardo Antoniol, economist with Bank of America in Milan.

However, many analysts thought he was being too cautious, with the financial markets showing resilience in the face of continued worries about the planned single European currency, and the lira itself gaining ground against the German mark.
"You can always find reasons to be cautious over monetary policy, but in my view there is no reason not to cut rates immediately," said Barbieri.
Antoniol agreed: "I think Fazio is being a bit cautious given the performance of the market. A half point cut wouldn't be disastrous," he said.
Fazio has taken to wrong-footing the market over the past year and some analysts suggested he might do the same now, with a swift cut this week.
Others expected him to wait to see preliminary June inflation data towards the end of the month, forecast to show another slight easing in price dynamics.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government, battling to tame state accounts, is anxiously awaiting another rate cut, with every percentage point fall in rates saving the Treasury an estimated 20 trillion lire ($11.8 billion) a year in lower interest payments on its debt mountain.
Prodi has also estimated that each percentage point fall saved Italian industry an annual seven trillion lire.

Figures released last week showed Italy's gross domestic product (GDP) fell 0.5 percent year-on-year in the first quarter of 1997. Business leaders have repeatedly called for a less restrictive monetary policy to help kick-start the economy.
